e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Nathan, from natan, he gave, understood as God has given. Nathan was the prophet who confronted King David; this spelling is also the Polish, Portuguese and Spanish one.
namesakes: Natan Sharansky (Soviet dissident and Israeli politician)

e.etymology: A respelling of Adeline, the French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal, noble.
A recent American coinage joining Ren, or the bird name Wren, to the -leigh ending. Renley and Wrenley are sister spellings.
A pet form of Martin, from Latin Martinus, of Mars, and less often of Martha or Martina. It was given as a name in its own right mostly in the 1950s and 1960s.
namesakes: Marty Robbins (country singer of El Paso)
Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman's character in Ozark)

assoc.t: Marty McFly, hero of Back to the Future

e.etymology: From Hebrew Shoshannah, lily, through Greek Sousanna. Susanna appears in the Apocrypha as a woman falsely accused and in Luke as a follower of Jesus.
A spelling of Arlen or Arlan, a name of uncertain origin that has been in American use since the late 1800s.
A respelling of Adalyn, a modern American form of Adeline, the French pet form of Adele, from Germanic adal, noble.
A Spanish and Portuguese name, especially common in Brazil, usually traced to the Germanic elements os or ans, god, and mar, famous.
A modern American coinage, the Tay- of Taylor with the -lee ending of Kaylee and Baylee.
From the diesel engine and its fuel, named for the German engineer Rudolf Diesel, who patented the engine in the 1890s. As a first name it is an American choice of the 2000s.

assoc.t: Vin Diesel, Fast & Furious actor, by stage surname
Diesel, Italian denim and fashion label

e.meaning: gold, truth or benevolence, depending on the language and character
e.etymology: A name shared by three languages. In Chinese it can be written with characters such as gold or advance, in Korean with truth or treasure, and in Japanese with benevolence.

assoc.t: Jin of BTS, K-pop singer Kim Seok-jin
Jin Kazama, lead fighter of the Tekken games

e.note: Sounds the same as gin, the liquor.

e.etymology: An African American name, a respelling of Davon in the family of Devon and Javon. The Chicago rapper King Von was born Dayvon Bennett.
namesakes: King Von (Chicago rapper, born Dayvon Bennett)

e.etymology: An anglicized form of Alasdair, the Scottish Gaelic form of Alexander, from Greek for defender of men. It is also the base of the surname McAllister.
A respelling of Kaia. In Scandinavia Kaia is a short form of Katarina; in the United States it is more often taken as a feminine form of Kai, Hawaiian for sea.
A modern American elaboration of Eva or Evie with the -anna ending of Arianna and Gianna.
A Breton name, the feminine of Ael, angel, from Latin angelus. Many English speakers know it from Aela the Huntress in the video game Skyrim; the similar Aella was an Amazon in Greek myth.

assoc.t: Aela the Huntress, warrior in the game Skyrim

e.etymology: From Frankish Hariberht, made up of hari, army, and berht, bright, brought to England by the Normans. It was a top American boys' name from the 1880s into the 1930s.
namesakes: Herbert Hoover (31st president of the United States)

assoc.t: Herbert, the creepy elderly neighbor on Family Guy

e.etymology: The French feminine diminutive of Antoine, the French form of Anthony, from the Roman family name Antonius, whose origin is unknown. Marie Antoinette made it famous.
namesakes: Marie Antoinette (queen of France executed in 1793)
Antoinette Perry (Broadway director, namesake of the Tony Awards)

assoc.t: Marie Antoinette, French queen guillotined in 1793

e.etymology: An African American coinage of the early 1990s, spread by DeVante Swing of the R&B group Jodeci. It follows the sound of Dante with a De- opening.
namesakes: DeVante Swing (founder and producer of the R&B group Jodeci)

e.etymology: A modern American elaboration of Shay or Shea with the -lee ending. Shea comes from the Irish surname Ó Séaghdha, from a byname meaning admirable or hawk-like.
From Sanskrit surya, the sun and the name of the Hindu sun god. The word is a distant cousin of English sun and Latin sol.
namesakes: Surya Bonaly (French figure skater famed for her one-bladed backflip)

e.etymology: Taken up in the US from Katara, the waterbending heroine of Avatar: The Last Airbender, first aired in 2005 and remade in live action for Netflix in 2024.

assoc.t: waterbender heroine of Avatar: The Last Airbender

e.note: Katara is the Greek word for curse.

e.etymology: From Arabic Mazin, linked to muzn, clouds that carry rain. It is also the name of an old Arab tribe, the Banu Mazin.
A respelling of Ryder, an English occupational surname for a mounted soldier or messenger, from Old English ridere.
A compound of Rosa, rose, and Bella, beautiful, in the Italian style, like Isabella and Annabella.
An English surname, a variant of Lock, for someone who lived by an enclosure or a river lock or who worked as a locksmith. It is best known from the philosopher John Locke.

assoc.t: John Locke, the man of faith on the TV series Lost

e.meaning: broad, generous or abundant, depending on the kanji
e.etymology: A Japanese name, also a short form of longer names such as Hiroshi and Hiroki. Hiro can be written with kanji meaning broad, generous, abundant or great.

assoc.t: Hiro Hamada, boy inventor of Disney's Big Hero 6
Hiro Nakamura, time traveler in the TV series Heroes

e.note: Said almost exactly like the English word hero.

e.etymology: A Latin American name, a variant of Keylor, which Costa Rican goalkeeper Keylor Navas made widely known. Its further origin is not documented.
A recent American coinage in the pattern of Kehlani and Leilani. The -lani ending is Hawaiian for sky or heaven.
A short form of Carmelo, the Italian and Spanish name from Mount Carmel, Hebrew for garden or orchard. Basketball's Carmelo Anthony and LaMelo Ball both go by Melo.

assoc.t: Melo, nickname of NBA stars Carmelo Anthony and LaMelo Ball

e.etymology: A variant of Roxana, from Greek Rhoxane, a name of Old Persian or Bactrian origin akin to Persian roshan, bright. Roxana was the Bactrian wife of Alexander the Great.

American use began with Steely Dan's 1977 album Aja, said like Asia; Donald Fagen said the title came from a Korean woman's name. Aja is also a Sanskrit name meaning unborn and a Yoruba forest spirit.
namesakes: Aja Naomi King (actress in How to Get Away with Murder)
A'ja Wilson (WNBA MVP and Olympic gold medalist, spelled A'ja)

assoc.t: A'ja Wilson, WNBA star and multiple-time MVP

e.note: The spelling does not show the pronunciation; most Americans say it like Asia.
